modal-dialog.modal-heading: The Premium Tax Credit (PTC)

modal-content.p: The PTC helps eligible people cover their premiums (monthly payments) for health insurance purchased through a government Marketplace like HealthCare.gov or a state Marketplace or exchange.
To get this credit, you must meet certain requirements and file a tax return with Form 8962, Premium Tax Credit (PTC).
Most people who qualify for the PTC get the credit in advance to help pay their monthly health insurance premiums throughout the year.
These advance payments of PTC are made by the Marketplace directly to the insurance provider on a person’s behalf.
When you file your taxes, the amount of the credit you got in advance is compared to the amount you actually qualify for.
If you didn’t get the full amount that you qualify for through advance payments, you’ll get the remaining credit when you file your taxes.
If your advance payments are more than the PTC you qualify for, you’ll have to repay some or all of the excess amount on your federal tax return.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Child and Dependent Care Credit (CDCC)

modal-content.p: The Child and Dependent Care Credit is a tax benefit that helps taxpayers who paid for the care of a family or household member while working or looking for work.
This credit is a percentage of your qualified child and dependent care expenses, and the percentage is based on your Adjusted Gross Income (AGI).

The credit ranges from % to % of your expenses up to for one qualifying person and for two qualifying people. This means the biggest credit you can get is for one qualifying person and for two or more qualifying people.
This credit is nonrefundable. This means that it can reduce your taxes, but it won’t reduce what you owe below $0. In other words, it can’t give you a refund.

There are some tax situations that Direct File doesn’t support yet. We ask questions to check if these situations apply to you as you complete your return. Also, if you or your spouse had dependent care provided in that you paid for later in , and you didn’t take the maximum amount of expenses for CDCC in , you won’t be able to use Direct File this year. This requires completing Worksheet A and line 9b of Form 2441.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Credit for the Elderly or the Disabled

modal-content.p: The Credit for the Elderly or the Disabled is a tax benefit that helps low-income taxpayers who meet either of the following criteria:

ul.li: Aged 65 or older
Retired on permanent and total disability and received certain types of taxable disability income

modal-content.p: Taxpayers who meet the eligibility requirements can qualify for the credit.
This credit is nonrefundable. This means that it can reduce your taxes, but it won’t reduce what you owe below $0. In other words, it can’t give you a refund.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Saver’s Credit (Retirement Savings Contributions Credit)

modal-content.p: The Saver’s Credit, also known as the Retirement Savings Contributions Credit, is a tax benefit for low- to moderate-income taxpayers that offsets a portion of workers’ voluntarily contributions to their Individual Retirement Arrangements (IRAs), 401(k) plans and similar workplace retirement programs. The Saver’s credit also helps eligible people who are the designated beneficiaries of an Achieving a Better Life Experience (ABLE) account.
Taxpayers who meet the eligibility requirements for the Saver’s Credit can qualify for up to ( if married filing jointly).
This credit is nonrefundable. This means that it can reduce your taxes, but it won’t reduce what you owe below $0. In other words, it can’t give you a refund.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Child Tax Credit (CTC) and Additional Child Tax Credit (ACTC)

modal-content.p: The Child Tax Credit and Additional Child Tax Credit are tax benefits that help families raising children. They are different parts of the same credit program. The total amount of these credits cannot be more than per child.
Taxpayers who meet the eligibility requirements for CTC can qualify for up to per child.
This credit is nonrefundable. This means that it can reduce your taxes, but it won’t reduce what you owe below $0. In other words, it can’t give you a refund.
For example, if you qualify for a $2,000 Child Tax Credit but you owe $1,000 in taxes, you can only reduce your taxes by $1,000, not the full $2,000.
ACTC is the refundable part of the credit, worth up to per child. A refundable credit will reduce your taxes. It can even result in a refund if it reduces your taxes below $0.
ACTC is available to taxpayers who qualify for CTC but couldn’t claim the full amount because they didn’t owe any taxes, or owed less than the amount of their CTC.

p.a: Learn more about CTC and ACTC

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Credit for Other Dependents (ODC)

modal-content.p: Taxpayers with dependents who don’t qualify for the Child Tax Credit may be able to claim the Credit for Other Dependents.
Taxpayers who meet the eligibility requirements for ODC can qualify for up to per dependent.
This credit is nonrefundable. This means that it can reduce your taxes, but it won’t reduce what you owe below $0. In other words, it can’t give you a refund.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC)

modal-content.p: The Earned Income Tax Credit is a tax benefit that helps low- to moderate-income workers and families.
You don’t need to have a qualifying child to qualify for EITC, though you may get a bigger credit if you do.
Taxpayers who meet the eligibility requirements for EITC can qualify for up to:

if they have one qualifying child with a valid SSN
if they have 2 qualifying children with valid SSNs

modal-content.p: This credit is refundable. A refundable credit will reduce your taxes. It can even result in a refund if it reduces your taxes below $0.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What are Forms 1095-B and 1095-C?

modal-content.p: Forms 1095-B and 1095-C are not related to Marketplace health plans. You don’t need these forms to file your federal tax return.

ul.li: Form 1095-B is used by health insurance providers to report information about people who have minimum essential coverage.
Form 1095-C is used by large employers with more than 50 full-time employees to report information about offers of health coverage and enrollment in health coverage for their employees.

modal-content.p: If for you only have Forms 1095-B or 1095-C and not Form 1095-A, then you probably didn’t have a Marketplace health plan that qualifies for the Premium Tax Credit (PTC).

modal-content.p: The Marketplace sends Form 1095-A, Health Insurance Marketplace Statement to people enrolled in qualified Marketplace health plans.

The Marketplace should mail or electronically provide the form before January 31, . If you don’t receive a Form 1095-A, or need to request a copy, then log in to your Marketplace account to download the form or contact your Marketplace for help.

If you got coverage through a state Marketplace like , visit their website to download or request a Form 1095-A.
Your Forms 1095-A will also be available in your IRS Online Account when the IRS receives them.

If someone else enrolled you, your spouse (who you’re filing jointly with), or a dependent, then a Form 1095-A may be sent to the person who completed the enrollment. You’ll need to check with them to get a copy.

modal-content.p: If no one on your tax return had a qualified Marketplace health plan, but someone received a Form 1095-A, the form may have been sent by mistake.

Before you file your taxes, you’ll need to contact HealthCare.gov or your state Marketplace to correct this mistake by getting a voided Form 1095-A. If you file your federal tax return without first getting a voided 1095-A, the IRS may reject your tax return.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What are advance payments of Premium Tax Credit (PTC)?

modal-content.p: When you enroll in a qualified Marketplace health plan, you estimate your expected income and family size for the year of coverage. modal-content.p: Certain government-sponsored health coverage is Minimum Essential Coverage (MEC). You generally can’t take the Premium Tax Credit (PTC) for a person in your tax family for any months when they were eligible for other MEC including:

ul.li: Someone pays the premiums on behalf of the person enrolled in the coverage before the federal tax filing deadline
The premiums are paid with advance payments of the Premium Tax Credit (PTC)

modal-content.p: For anyone who had a successful eligibility appeal, became eligible for advance payments of PTC, and retroactively enrolled in a qualified Marketplace health plan:

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What’s Minimum Essential Coverage (MEC)?

modal-content.p: Certain government-sponsored health coverage is Minimum Essential Coverage (MEC). You generally can’t take the Premium Tax Credit (PTC) for a person in your tax family for any months when they were eligible for other MEC including:

ul.li: Medicaid (except for certain limited scope programs)
Medicare Part A
Medicare Advantage plans
The Children’s Health Insurance Program (CHIP)
The Department of Veterans Affairs medical benefits package for eligible veterans
Civilian Health and Medical Program of the Department of Veterans Affairs (CHAMPVA)
Comprehensive health care for children suffering from spina bifida who are the children of Vietnam veterans and veterans of covered service in Korea
TRICARE
Health coverage for Peace Corps volunteers
Other health coverage designated by the Department of Health and Human Services

modal-content.p: Individual market coverage is considered MEC, but if someone was enrolled in or eligible for individual market coverage, they can still qualify for the PTC.

A person’s eligibility for Medicaid or CHIP is decided when they enroll in the qualified health plan. That eligibility decision applies for the entire year (even if your family size or household income changes).

You:

modal-dialog.modal-heading: The Premium Tax Credit (PTC)

modal-content.p: The PTC helps eligible people cover their premiums (monthly payments) for health insurance purchased through a government Marketplace like HealthCare.gov or a state Marketplace or exchange.
To get this credit, you must meet certain requirements and file a tax return with Form 8962, Premium Tax Credit (PTC).
Most people who qualify for the PTC get the credit in advance to help pay their monthly health insurance premiums throughout the year.
These advance payments of PTC are made by the Marketplace directly to the insurance provider on a person’s behalf.
When you file your taxes, the amount of the credit you got in advance is compared to the amount you actually qualify for.
If you didn’t get the full amount that you qualify for through advance payments, you’ll get the remaining credit when you file your taxes.
If your advance payments are more than the PTC you qualify for, you’ll have to repay some or all of the excess amount on your federal tax return.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What are advance payments of Premium Tax Credit (PTC)?

modal-content.p: When you enroll in a qualified Marketplace health plan, you estimate your expected income and family size for the year of coverage. Based on this information, the Marketplace estimates the amount of monthly PTC you’ll be allowed for the year of coverage. You can then decide to use any amount of PTC in advance to lower your monthly health insurance premiums.
Most people who qualify for the PTC choose to get it in advance to help pay their monthly health insurance premiums throughout the year.
These advance payments of PTC are made by the Marketplace directly to the insurance provider on a person’s behalf.
Advance payments are sometimes referred to as a "subsidy," "tax credit," or "APTC."
Learn more about advance payments of PTC.

modal-content.p: When calculating how much excess advance Premium Tax Credit (PTC) you’ll need to repay, the IRS uses repayment limitations shown in Table 5 of the instructions for Form 8962.
Your repayment of excess advance PTC may be limited (lowered) if your household income is below 400% of the federal poverty line for your family size.

modal-content.p: The Child and Dependent Care Credit is a tax benefit that helps taxpayers who paid for the care of a family or household member while working or looking for work.

This credit is nonrefundable. This means that it can reduce your taxes, but it won’t reduce what you owe below $0. In other words, it can’t give you a refund.

If you don’t have the IP PIN, you have another filing option: you can file a paper federal tax return. Note, the IRS will need to review your paper federal tax return to check your identity. This review process could delay any refund.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What is an Identity Protection (IP) PIN?

modal-content.p: The IRS IP PIN is a 6-digit number assigned to eligible individuals to help prevent the misuse of their Social Security number or Individual Taxpayer Identification Number on fraudulent federal income tax returns. A new IP PIN will be generated each year.

If the IRS assigned you (or anyone on your tax return) an IP PIN, you must use it to confirm your identity on any return filed during the current calendar year. This includes current year returns as well as any delinquent tax returns.
If you don’t already have an IP PIN, you may get an IP PIN as a proactive step to protect yourself from tax-related identity theft.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: What if I file my federal tax return without the IRS-assigned Identity Protection (IP) PIN?

modal-content.p: If the IRS assigned you (or anyone on your federal tax return) an IP PIN, you must use it to confirm your or their identities on your federal tax return.
If you file your federal tax return electronically without the IRS-assigned IP PIN, your federal tax return will get rejected.

Alternative federal tax filing option
If you don’t have the IP PIN, you have another filing option: you can file a paper federal tax return. Note, the IRS will need to review your paper federal tax return to check your identity. This review process could delay any refund.

If you need to file a paper federal tax return, you can still use Direct File to fill out your tax return. You would need to then print out your forms to mail to the IRS. Learn about the steps to file by paper.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: The Premium Tax Credit (PTC)

modal-content.p: The PTC helps eligible people cover their premiums (monthly payments) for health insurance purchased through a government Marketplace like HealthCare.gov or a state Marketplace or exchange.
To get this credit, you must meet certain requirements and file a tax return with Form 8962, Premium Tax Credit (PTC).
Most people who qualify for the PTC get the credit in advance to help pay their monthly health insurance premiums throughout the year.
These advance payments of PTC are made by the Marketplace directly to the insurance provider on a person’s behalf.
When you file your taxes, the amount of the credit you got in advance is compared to the amount you actually qualify for.
If you didn’t get the full amount that you qualify for through advance payments, you’ll get the remaining credit when you file your taxes.
If your advance payments are more than the PTC you qualify for, you’ll have to repay some or all of the excess amount on your federal tax return.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Child and Dependent Care Credit (CDCC)

modal-content.p: The Child and Dependent Care Credit is a tax benefit that helps taxpayers who paid for the care of a family or household member while working or looking for work.
This credit is a percentage of your qualified child and dependent care expenses, and the percentage is based on your Adjusted Gross Income (AGI).

The credit ranges from % to % of your expenses up to for one qualifying person and for two qualifying people. This means the biggest credit you can get is for one qualifying person and for two or more qualifying people.
This credit is nonrefundable. This means that it can reduce your taxes, but it won’t reduce what you owe below $0. In other words, it can’t give you a refund.

modal-dialog.modal-heading: Child Tax Credit (CTC) and Additional Child Tax Credit (ACTC)

modal-content.p: The Child Tax Credit and Additional Child Tax Credit are tax benefits that help families raising children. They are different parts of the same credit program. The total amount of these credits cannot be more than per child.
Taxpayers who meet the eligibility requirements for CTC can qualify for up to per child.
This credit is nonrefundable. This means that it can reduce your taxes, but it won’t reduce what you owe below $0. In other words, it can’t give you a refund.
For example, if you qualify for a $2,000 Child Tax Credit but you owe $1,000 in taxes, you can only reduce your taxes by $1,000, not the full $2,000.
ACTC is the refundable part of the credit, worth up to per child. A refundable credit will reduce your taxes. It can even result in a refund if it reduces your taxes below $0.
ACTC is available to taxpayers who qualify for CTC but couldn’t claim the full amount because they didn’t owe any taxes, or owed less than the amount of their CTC.

modal-content.p: The Earned Income Tax Credit is a tax benefit that helps low- to moderate-income workers and families.
You don’t need to have a qualifying child to qualify for EITC, though you may get a bigger credit if you do.
